working_title: Electric vs Push Golf Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: A practical, opinionated decision guide for the regular UK walker who is weighing up whether the jump to an electric trolley is genuinely worth it, or whether a quality three-wheel push trolley still makes more sense for their game, course terrain, and boot space. The post cuts through the marketing noise by anchoring the decision in real UK-specific factors: hilly links terrain, damp conditions, car park practicalities, and frequency of play.
research_notes:
- Two dominant UK electric trolley brands are Motocaddy and PowaKaddy, both well-established and regularly topping UK best-seller lists (Motocaddy S1, PowaKaddy CT6 among the most cited models for 2026)
- Electric trolley price range in UK market runs from roughly £499 (Motocaddy SE, cited as best-value entry-level from a major brand) up to £749 for PowaKaddy CT6, and £1,249+ for GPS flagship models such as PowaKaddy CT12
- Push trolleys are cheaper, lighter, fold more compactly, and typically include more onboard storage than electric equivalents; trade-off is the physical effort required, especially on hills
- Three-wheel push trolleys are the standard recommendation over two-wheel pull models: pushing weight ahead of you is easier on the body than twisting to pull behind
- Avoid old-fashioned two-wheel pull trolleys — noted by multiple sources as putting uneven strain on one side of the body
- Electric trolleys make most sense for: frequent walkers (weekly+), hilly home courses, golfers with back or joint concerns
- Push trolleys suit: flatter courses, occasional golfers, those short on boot or storage space at home, those on tighter budgets
- Push trolleys fold more compactly than electric models due to absence of motor/battery hardware
- Electric trolleys need charging between rounds and should be stored somewhere dry — a practical consideration for UK garages
- Battery life on entry-level electric models is typically rated to 18 holes; some mid/upper models rate to 36 holes
- Features on electric models that are worth noting (without fabricating specs): GPS integration, downhill control (DHC on Motocaddy range), remote/follow modes on premium models (e.g. Stewart Golf Q Follow uses Bluetooth to follow the golfer hands-free)
- Storage is a genuine push trolley advantage — electric trolleys often require accessories to be bought separately
- Key frame material for push trolleys: aluminium (common balance of weight, strength, price); Clicgear 4.0 uses aircraft-grade aluminium
- Foot brake is a practical must-have feature for courses with slopes or raised tees
- Adjustable handle height worth checking before buying
- UK-specific nuance: many links and heathland courses are undulating — this tilts the value case toward electric more than a flat parkland course would
- No invented prices beyond what sources provided; do not state specific prices for any model as prices fluctuate and are only partially confirmed
